dedupe_keys.name: benefit cost of moore oklahoma s enhanced residential building code for tornadoes after the 20 may 2013 tornado

description: This case study evaluates whether the stronger residential building code adopted by the City of Moore, Oklahoma, after the tornado of 20 May 2013 pays for itself. That tornado devastated more than 1,000 homes, and in the following year the city adopted 12 modifications to its residential code. The study, by Xinyang Wu and Guangzhao Chen of Texas Tech University, is published in Advances in Wind Engineering (December 2025). Because earlier benefit-cost analyses relied on insured losses, the authors built a Monte Carlo tornado loss model combining tornado hazard modelling, fragility functions for enhanced and unenhanced houses, and local exposure data. The modifications reduce expected community losses; without discounting the benefit-cost ratio (mitigated loss over retrofit cost) is 0.88. Coverage: residential buildings in Moore, Oklahoma. Access: open-access journal article. Licence: CC BY-NC-ND per the open-access record; free to read. Caveats: only house construction losses are counted, so contents, injury and death losses would raise the ratio; the model and data are described in the article, not released separately. Simulation uses: evidence and a method for appraising wind-resistant building codes in tornado risk models. Related records: the wood-frame flood fragility data and the empirical hurricane vulnerability curves.
name: Benefit-cost of Moore, Oklahoma's enhanced residential building code for tornadoes (after the 20 May 2013 tornado)
organisations: Texas Tech University (Xinyang Wu, Guangzhao Chen)
outcomes: The simulated loss reduction from Moore's 12 code modifications gave a benefit-cost ratio of 0.88 without discounting, counting only house construction losses; the authors expect the ratio to rise if contents, injuries and deaths are included.
resources_used: Tornado fragility functions for enhanced and unenhanced houses
